<reason>CON won by making the kind-of-harm comparison easier to vote on: a nationally trusted credential concentrates attacker payoff and builds a queryable checkpoint architecture, unlike SSNs that prove little until paired with forgeries. PRO’s present-versus-contingent frame was the right motion rule, but it flattened that distinction, treated a funded-paper statute as a full stop to mandate creep, and never neutralized the incentive path from optional fast lane to de facto obligation. Both sides were disciplined and format-clean; A’s weighing of reimbursable diffuse fraud against a generative, hard-to-undo index was the cleaner path to victory.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A’s reply that optionality dies by delay and private demand (the SSN path), and that a stolen payment is finite while a trusted digital credential is generative until the victim wins a help-desk race.</best_rebuttal>
